clue.text: Radar distortions beginning to fall off in listening device

indicators.note: a distortion bends things out of shape, so the remaining letters are twisted into a new order
the first letter of the word distortions drops away before anything else happens

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then losing its opening letter

explanation.surface: Interference on a radar screen is put down to something fading in a bugging device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distortions' does double duty: it is part of the fodder, minus its D, and also the signal to rearrange RADAR plus ISTORTIONS.
explanation.definitionFit: A transistor radio is a small portable receiver people hold to their ear for broadcasts, so it is literally equipment for hearing.

clue.text: Large amount of buzz, then feeling less

parts.note: to give someone a buzz is to ring them up
more numb, with less sensation

explanation.surface: A loud electrical hum leaves someone tingling and then numb.
explanation.walkthrough: NUMBER here is the comparative of numb, not the noun. 'Telephone numbers' is informal British for a huge sum, especially a salary or price.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum described as a telephone number has so many digits it resembles a dialling code, hence colloquially a huge figure.

clue.text: Increase in gold federal agents start to tackle

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
G-men is American slang for FBI agents

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept from tackle

parts.note: the opening letter of tackle

explanation.surface: A rise in gold-smuggling has the FBI starting to tackle it.
explanation.definitionFit: To augment something is to make it bigger or add to it, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Violent blow from South Ham not hot

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south

indicators.note: not hot tells you to strip out the letter standing for hot

parts.note: a hock is a joint of ham from a pig's leg
H is the standard abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Reads like a London football fan describing a nasty tackle from a West Ham player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South Ham' suggests West Ham football club; Ham is in fact a hock, losing H. A sock in the jaw is a hard punch.
explanation.definitionFit: Sock is informal for a hard punch, as in a sock on the jaw, so it names a forceful strike.

clue.text: Occasionally supply incitement to spend a lot

indicators.note: occasionally means every so often, so only every other letter of supply is kept

parts.note: first, third and fifth letters of supply
an urge is a spur or prompting

explanation.surface: Now and then a supply of encouragement tempts a shopper into extravagance.
explanation.definitionFit: To splurge is to indulge in lavish spending, so the verb phrase about heavy outlay is a direct equivalent.

clue.text: Structural failing in cargo

indicators.note: something failing is collapsing out of shape, so the following letters fall into a different order

parts.note: taken as written, all seven letters

explanation.surface: An engineer reports a structural fault inside a cargo hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failing' looks like part of the definition, describing a structural failure, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Organic can mean belonging to the fundamental constitution of something, as in an organic part of the whole.

clue.text: Old character last to retire after career

indicators.note: after places the single kept letter behind the word for career

parts.note: to career is to run headlong

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of retire and no other

parts.note: final letter of retire

explanation.surface: An old-timer decides at last to retire after a long working life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old character' wants to be a veteran person, but it means an ancient letter; 'career' is the verb, to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: Runes are letters of the ancient Germanic alphabets, so each one is an old written symbol.

clue.text: Bored king badly engaged in half-hearted exploit

indicators.note: being engaged in something means being held inside it
half of the heart goes, so one of the two central letters of exploit is dropped

parts.note: a deed is a feat or exploit
R for rex, Latin for king
ill as an adverb means badly

explanation.surface: A weary monarch is clumsily caught up in a feeble escapade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bored' suggests weariness, matching the surface, but it is the past tense of bore, to make a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: To bore a hole and to drill one are the same action, so both past forms describe a hole made.

clue.text: Detective's easy task, Sudanese chap not devious

indicators.note: a devious route wanders off the straight path, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: An investigator finds an honest man from Sudan makes for simple work.
explanation.definitionFit: An investigation with an obvious outcome needing little effort is called this idiom, the kind a detective solves quickly.

clue.text: Thinking correctly, soldier goes into pub

indicators.note: going into a place puts one thing inside another

parts.note: your local is your neighbourhood pub
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier with sound judgement heads into the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is the British name for the pub nearest your home that you use regularly.
explanation.definitionFit: Logical describes reasoning that follows valid steps, so someone being logical reasons soundly.

clue.text: Real information I put in French article

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

indicators.note: putting something in places it inside the following word

parts.note: une is the French feminine for a
taken as written

explanation.surface: Authentic news is inserted into a French newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' suggests a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article; gen is British slang for the facts.
explanation.definitionFit: Something genuine is authentic and not fake, a direct adjective synonym.

clue.text: Some people always making excuse

indicators.note: some of the words means only a part of the run of letters is wanted

parts.note: spans the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A grumble about certain people who forever make excuses.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea can be a pretext offered in defence, as in a plea of ignorance, so it serves as justification.

clue.text: Cut of meat changing hands for stamp

indicators.note: hands are left and right, so changing hands swaps the L for an R

parts.note: flank is a cut of beef from the belly side

explanation.surface: A butcher's cut being traded for a postage stamp.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R are the abbreviations for left and right, the two hands.
explanation.definitionFit: To frank a letter is to mark it with an official postmark showing postage paid, the equivalent of stamping it.

clue.text: Green area on feminine, tiny jumper

indicators.note: on means placed after here, so the meadow word follows the single letter

parts.note: F is the grammatical abbreviation for feminine
a lea is a meadow or grassy field

explanation.surface: A clothes label: a green garment from the women's section, a tiny jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' is British for a sweater, which suits the fashion surface, but here it means something that jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleas are minute insects famous for leaping huge distances, making them small hopping creatures.

clue.text: In prison, do unending scrounge

indicators.note: in the prison means held inside the word for a jail

parts.note: a cage confines like a jail

indicators.note: without its ending, the final letter of do is cut off

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to an inmate serving an endless sentence: beg what you can.
explanation.definitionFit: To cadge is to obtain something by begging or imposing on others, the same as sponging or mooching.

clue.text: Instant gain for artist

parts.note: mo is short for moment
to net is to gain or clear as profit

explanation.surface: A painter makes an overnight profit, perhaps by selling a canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: Mo, as in 'half a mo', is British shorthand for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Claude Monet was the French Impressionist painter of the water lilies series.

clue.text: Destroy cycling film's unreleased snippet

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round from the front to the back like a wheel turning

parts.note: to take out is to eliminate or destroy

explanation.surface: Wrecking a bicycle scene meant the footage never made the final cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The block is a two-word phrase whose halves swap places when the front half is moved round to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: An outtake is a filmed scene left out of the released version, a clip that never reached the public.

clue.text: Busy bird absolutely hasn't advanced

parts.note: a crow is a black bird

indicators.note: hasn't means is without, so the letter for advanced is removed

parts.note: dead as an intensifier, as in dead right
A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A level

explanation.surface: A frantic bird has stubbornly made no headway at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A busy street or room is one full of people, packed and thronged.

clue.text: Soldiers, leaderless, recruit second officers

indicators.note: without a leader the first letter of the soldiers word is lost

parts.note: men as in officers and men, the ranks
to sign up a player is to recruit them
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Troops without a commander take on a deputy as their officers.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is a junior commissioned rank in the navy, so ensigns are a kind of commissioned personnel.

clue.text: Rag turned up for wrapping round car part

parts.note: a rag is a tabloid newspaper, here The Sun

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning a word up reads it from bottom to top
wrapping something puts it inside a covering

parts.note: taken as written
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A tatty cloth gets tucked around a piece of a vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rag' looks like a cleaning cloth but is the British slang for a downmarket paper; The Sun is a UK tabloid.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunroof is a panel in a car's roof that slides or tilts open, a component of the vehicle body.

clue.text: US hospital department abandoning transport for wounded is exaggeration

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving behind, so those letters are dropped from the word

parts.note: a stretcher carries the injured
ER is the American emergency room

explanation.surface: Claims that a US emergency room has abandoned its stretchers are overblown.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch can mean an overstatement, as in saying that is a bit of a stretch, a claim beyond the truth.

clue.text: Cat fraud overheard

indicators.note: overheard means caught by ear, so the word is judged by its pronunciation

parts.note: a fraud is a cheater, which in non-rhotic speech matches the big cat

explanation.surface: A conman's scheme involving a cat is discovered by eavesdropping.
explanation.definitionFit: The cheetah is a big wild feline of Africa, the fastest land animal, so a member of the cat family.

clue.text: Perceive dread, we hear, in mythological creature

indicators.note: we hear says the words are to be taken by their sound

parts.note: to scent is to perceive by smell, and awe is reverent dread

explanation.surface: People report sensing terror in a legendary beast.
explanation.definitionFit: A centaur in Greek legend has a man's upper body on a horse's body, a creature of myth.

clue.text: Steal banks of their river, right?

indicators.note: the banks of a river are its edges, so only the outer letters of their are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of their
the Ouse is a river in England
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether to pilfer from the riverbanks belonging to others.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ouse is a river running through York in England.
explanation.definitionFit: To trouser money is British slang for pocketing it, often dishonestly, so it means to take what is not yours.

clue.text: Doctor Lauren not about to produce bone

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the name is rearranged
not tells you to leave out the letters meaning about

parts.note: taken as written
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A physician named Lauren, absent from her rounds, presents an X-ray of a bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a title for Lauren but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The ulna is one of the two long bones of the human forearm, on the little-finger side.

clue.text: Lying about after run during exercise

indicators.note: during places this pair inside the exercise letters, as something happening within

parts.note: PE is physical education

indicators.note: after puts the word for about behind the letter for run

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
on can mean about, as in a talk on art

explanation.surface: Lounging around after a jog during a workout.
explanation.definitionFit: Prone means lying face downward, so it describes a body stretched flat.

clue.text: Drink pint from either end?

indicators.note: the end at each side of the word pint leaves just its first and last letters

parts.note: the two ends of pint
or as in either this or that

explanation.surface: A puzzled drinker wonders which end of the glass to sip from.
explanation.walkthrough: The ends of pint stand either side of OR, so the clue reads 'pint ends with either between'.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a sweet fortified wine from Portugal, an after-dinner alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Just amazing diamond easily tops ornamental stone

indicators.note: in a down clue the tops of words are their first letters

parts.note: first letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Praise for a jewel that simply outshines even diamond.
explanation.definitionFit: Jade is a green mineral carved into jewellery and decorative objects, a semi-precious gem.

clue.text: Open goods taken from setter

indicators.note: taken from means removed out of the following word

parts.note: a setter is a breed of gundog
goods read as G's, two of the letter G for good

explanation.surface: Merchandise unwrapped and handed over by the compiler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' suggests the crossword compiler, but it is the dog; G is a standard abbreviation for good.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo a parcel or button is to unfasten it, so the verb means to open.

clue.text: Cheerful lad, soldier embracing uniform

indicators.note: embracing means holding within, so the letter for uniform goes inside the lad

parts.note: a lad is a boy
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
a soldier ant is a worker type in a colony

explanation.surface: A happy young man hugs a soldier dressed in uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: Buoyant moods are light and optimistic, as if floating, so it means upbeat and happy.

clue.text: Returning from Calais en masse, French souvenir lost?

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the letters are read from right to left
from means taken out of the run of words that follows

parts.note: spans the end of Calais, all of en and the start of masse

explanation.surface: Day-trippers coming home from Calais in a crowd have mislaid their souvenirs.
explanation.walkthrough: Souvenir is French for memory, so a French souvenir lost is memory loss; the question mark flags the twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Amnesia is loss of memory, and the French word souvenir means a memory or recollection.

clue.text: Mobile rescuers here for training update

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A mobile rescue team turns up for on-the-job instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' looks like a link word but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A refresher course brings someone's skills or knowledge back up to date, a short programme of instruction.
